title: Joshua 2:15–24
context: Rahab lets the spies down by a cord through her window, because her house is on the side of the wall. She tells them to hide in the mountain three days until the pursuers return. The men bind the oath to a visible sign: she must tie the line of scarlet thread in that same window and gather her father’s household into the house; anyone who goes out into the street dies at his own risk, and if she talks about their business they are free of the oath. She agrees, sends them away, and ties the scarlet line in the window. After three days they return to Joshua and report that the LORD has truly delivered the land into Israel’s hands, and that the inhabitants melt away. Both traditions read the sign and the gathering into the house as the terms of the sworn kindness, and her immediate tying of the line as faith acting on the word. A common historic Christian reading has seen the scarlet cord as a type of Christ’s blood, sometimes compared with the Passover mark on the door; that typology is a traditional interpretive option, not a demonstrated consensus, and it is not a point of Arminian–Reformed contrast. The spies’ report echoes Rahab’s own confession that the LORD has already given the land.

verses.text: Then she let them down by a cord through the window; for her house was on the side of the wall, and she lived on the wall.
verses.arminianNotes:
She lets them down by a cord through the window, because her house was on the side of the wall and she lived on the wall. The same house that hid them now becomes their way out of the shut city.

Arminian readers hear a further costly act. She does not only speak well of Israel; she uses her house’s place on the wall to send the messengers out another way.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the architectural note as the narrative gives it: her house was “on the side of the wall,” which made a window-escape possible. The text does not here describe the later fall of the wall, and both traditions can wait for chapter 6 for that.

Both traditions read the letting-down as part of the help James later names, without settling later questions about how this house stood when the wall fell.

verses.text: She said to them, “Go to the mountain, lest the pursuers find you. Hide yourselves there three days, until the pursuers have returned. Afterward, you may go your way.”
verses.arminianNotes:
She tells them to go to the mountain, hide themselves there three days until the pursuers have returned, and then go their way, lest the pursuers find them.

Arminian readers hear wise, practical care. She continues to protect them after they leave her house, and they will have to follow this counsel if the escape is to hold.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note the three days and the mountain as her instruction, not as a new word from Joshua. The pursuers have gone toward the fords; she sends the spies the other way until that search is over.

Both traditions take the counsel as part of her sending them out in safety, and the next verses will show that it worked.

verses.text: The men said to her, “We will be guiltless of this your oath which you’ve made us to swear.
verses.arminianNotes:
The men say they will be guiltless of the oath she has made them swear. The terms that follow will define when the oath binds them and when it does not.

Arminian readers hear a careful, moral seriousness about the vow. An oath in the LORD’s name is not casual, and both sides need to know its terms.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise hear the men clarifying the oath before they depart. They do not dismiss the pledge; they define the conditions under which they would be free of it.

Both traditions take the verse as the introduction to those conditions, not as a refusal of the kindness already promised.

verses.text: Behold, when we come into the land, tie this line of scarlet thread in the window which you used to let us down. Gather to yourself into the house your father, your mother, your brothers, and all your father’s household.
verses.arminianNotes:
When they come into the land, she is to tie “this line of scarlet thread” in the window by which she let them down, and to gather her father, mother, brothers, and all her father’s household into the house.

Arminian readers hear a visible sign and a gathered family. The line marks the house, and the household must actually come inside if they are to share the promised mercy. Some Christian readers have also seen in the scarlet line a type of Christ’s blood; that is a historic interpretive option, not required by the verse itself.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same two conditions: the scarlet line in that window, and the family gathered into that house. The sign belongs to the oath; it is a true token of the kindness already sworn.

That typological reading is common in the history of interpretation, sometimes compared with the Passover blood on the door, but it is not a demonstrated consensus and is not a point of contrast between the two traditions. Both take the line as the sworn sign that marks the house for mercy.

verses.text: It shall be that whoever goes out of the doors of your house into the street, his blood will be on his head, and we will be guiltless. Whoever is with you in the house, his blood shall be on our head, if any hand is on him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Whoever goes out of the doors of the house into the street, his blood will be on his own head, and the spies will be guiltless. Whoever stays in the house, his blood will be on the spies’ head if any hand is on him.

Arminian readers hear personal responsibility inside the oath. The protection is real, and it is located in the marked house; leaving it is a choice that bears its own risk.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note the same allocation of blood-guilt. The spies accept liability for those who remain inside, and they are free of it if someone goes out. The house, under the sign, is the place of the promised safety.

Some readers have noticed a resemblance to the Passover charge to stay inside the marked house; that parallel is a possible comparison, not a claim the narrator makes here. Both traditions agree on the terms themselves.

verses.text: But if you talk about this business of ours, then we shall be guiltless of your oath which you’ve made us to swear.”
verses.arminianNotes:
If she talks about this business of theirs, they will be guiltless of her oath. Silence, already named in verse 14, is restated as a condition of the pledge.

Arminian readers hear that the kindness is not automatic. She has asked for a sworn mercy, and she must keep the confidence that belongs to it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the condition as part of the same oath, not as a withdrawal of it. If the business is made known, the men are free of the bond she made them swear.

Both traditions read the verse as a real term of the covenant kindness, shared ground with verses 14 and 17.

verses.text: She said, “Let it be as you have said.” She sent them away, and they departed. Then she tied the scarlet line in the window.
verses.arminianNotes:
She answers, “Let it be as you have said.” She sends them away, and then she ties the scarlet line in the window, before the city has fallen and before the spies have even reached Joshua.

Arminian readers hear faith acting at once. She agrees to the terms and puts the sign in place. James later asks whether she was not “justified by works when she received the messengers and sent them out another way”.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise stress the immediate tying of the line. The sign is not left for a later day; her deed matches her word, which Hebrews 11:31 frames as receiving the spies in peace, and which James does not set against that faith.

Both traditions hold Hebrews 11:31 and James 2:25 together here: her faith is real, and it is shown in what she does. That shared reading of Rahab does not require settling the wider justification debate in this verse.

verses.text: They went and came to the mountain, and stayed there three days, until the pursuers had returned. The pursuers sought them all along the way, but didn’t find them.
verses.arminianNotes:
They go to the mountain and stay there three days, until the pursuers have returned. The pursuers seek them all along the way and do not find them.

Arminian readers hear that her counsel was true. The three days and the mountain hide them, and the search fails; her wisdom, and God’s care, bring the men through.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the pursuers seek and do not find. The mission survives by the path she gave them, and the LORD’s purpose to bring word back to Joshua is not overturned by the king’s search.

Both traditions take the verse as the outworking of verse 16, shared narrative ground.

verses.text: Then the two men returned, descended from the mountain, crossed the river, and came to Joshua the son of Nun. They told him all that had happened to them.
verses.arminianNotes:
The two men return, descend from the mountain, cross the river, and come to Joshua son of Nun. They tell him all that had happened to them.

Arminian readers hear a complete report, not a trimmed one. Joshua is to lead on the basis of what God has actually done in Jericho, including the unexpected faith they found there.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the return to Joshua. The secret mission ends in testimony to the appointed leader, and “all that had happened to them” includes Rahab’s confession and the oath, not only the city’s layout.

Both traditions take the verse as the spies discharging their charge by a full report.

verses.text: They said to Joshua, “Truly the LORD has delivered all the land into our hands. Moreover, all the inhabitants of the land melt away before us.”
verses.arminianNotes:
They say to Joshua, “Truly the LORD has delivered all the land into our hands. Moreover, all the inhabitants of the land melt away before us.”

Arminian readers hear the spies now confessing what Rahab had already said. Their report is faith’s agreement with her knowledge, and it is meant to strengthen Joshua and the people for the crossing.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress “has delivered” and the echo of “melt away”. The report is not merely military intelligence; it is a confession that the LORD has already given the land, matching Rahab’s “I know that the LORD has given you the land,” already spoken on the roof.

Both traditions take the closing words as shared ground with Rahab’s confession and with the promises of chapter 1: the land is the LORD’s gift, and fear has already fallen on its inhabitants.
